articles.body:
For a brief moment on Tuesday night, the Victorian election looked like it might actually get interesting.

Two weeks into the offical campaign, with early voting opening on Wednesday, the contest has been pretty short on excitement. The Labor government has continued to slide in the polls, while the Coalition opposition has largely been focused on not getting in its own way for long enough to cruise to victory.

But the only debate of the campaign offered a welcome jolt of life. Dubbed the “People’s Forum” by hosts News24 and the Herald Sun, Tuesday evening’s showdown delivered a few moments of political theatre.

There was the moment the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, mocked the premier, Ben Carroll, for refusing to say the names of his predecessors, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, telling the Labor leader they’re “not Voldemort”.

“I can say their name just as you can say Jeff Kennett’s name,” Carroll responded.

“Jeff Kennett,” Wilson immediately retorted.

(For all the back-and-forth, Carroll never did say their names).

Or Wilson’s apparent “Julia Gillard moment”, according to the Herald Sun, when she told Carroll she “would not be lectured” by him on the costings of her policies. The premier had claimed the Liberal plans didn’t “stack up” and would require cuts to healthcare funding to pay down debt.

“I like to see these scare campaigns that you run,” Wilson said. “But Ben, I won’t be lectured by you or your government on costings when you have racked up $200bn worth of debt in this state.”

Then there was One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who said the state resembled “Gotham City” because of rising crime and vowed to lock up more offenders – even if that meant sending them interstate.

“I don’t give a damn if our prisons are full. You’ve broken the law. You’re going to jail. They’re bringing in a supermax in New South Wales. That’s where you’re bloody going,” he said.

The only person to receive rousing applause was Billy, a bearded schoolteacher who asked how the leaders planned to rebuild trust in politics when, as he put it: “Nobody believes a word you say any more – and it’s fundamental. No fun, and mostly mental.”

But many of the night’s most memorable moments came courtesy of Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, whose late inclusion on the panel followed a stoush between Carroll and Wilson over whether Pickering should be invited.

“Having four of us on the stage tonight tells you everything about how politics is changing,” Sandell told the 100 undecided voters gathered at the Sofitel in Melbourne.

In her green blazer, and unmistakably in enemy territory, Sandell spoke authentically and was the only leader willing to take all three other parties to task: Labor over donations from the gambling industry, the Liberals over money from property developers and One Nation for its links to billionaire Gina Rinehart, who she said is “writing [their] policy”.

“If you’re wondering why you can’t afford your groceries or your rent or to buy a home, just look at who is funding these three other parties,” Sandell said.

When offered the opportunity to ask any other leader a question, Sandell asked Carroll how he can claim to fight for working people given cuts to the public sector and fights with health workers, teachers, council workers and firefighters over wages.

She also engaged in a back and forth with Wilson on several issues. Asked whether she would possibly support the Liberals with confidence and supply in the event of a hung parliament, she said the Greens values were “quite far apart” from the Coalition’s: “Jess Wilson wants to rip up treaty. She wants to rip up renewable energy. She wants to make sigfniciant cuts to public service.”

Wilson relied on an often repeated line that treaty “goes far further than what the voice [to parliament] ever did” and “undermines our parliament”.

Sandell’s response: “You know that’s not true though, you can’t lie to the Victorian people like that.”

The pair also clashed over pro-Palestinian protests in Melbourne’s CBD, with Sandell defending the right to “peaceful protest”.

“There is a very clear difference between antisemitism, which is unacceptable, and actually standing up and calling out war crimes that are happening by the government of Israel,” she said.

Wilson responded: “At these protests, we have seen people throw rocks at police officers. That is not a peaceful protest.

Sandell responded that existing laws already dealt with such incidents and argued that protest permits were not the answer.

“Politicians shouldn’t be the ones deciding who gets to protest,” she said. “That is an authoritarian government move, and we do not want that.”

Pickering agreed with Sandell and said politicians should not be deciding who gets to protest. He described One Nation as a “flagbearer” for the principles of democracy, including freedom of speech.

“I don’t necessarily think the permits are the way to go,” he said.

Wilson, who holds a comfortable lead in the polls, arguably had the most to lose from the debate but held her own. She largely avoided taking the bait from the other leaders, including Pickering, who during his turn to ask a question, tried to pressure her on the Coalition’s position on legislated net zero targets. Wilson stuck to her line that she was governed by “practicality” and “not ideology”.

She was less definitive on the Suburban Rail Loop, leaving open the possibility of scrapping the multibillion-dollar project once the Coalition had “visibility” of the contracts that have been signed.

Asked by moderator Kieran Gilbert if the Coalition would be willing to scrap the project and move on, Wilson said: “That’s exactly what the review is for.”

Carroll, meanwhile, acknowledged that Labor had made mistakes during its 12 years in government but leaned heavily on its record, including 121 new schools, record NAPLAN results, the highest-paid teachers in the country and 17,000 nurses.

He also repeatedly referred to his decision to call a royal commission into allegations of corruption on government construction sites, describing it as one of the “hardest” things he had done.

Victoria will not get another leaders debate, after Carroll and Wilson failed to agree on terms for one on free-to-air television.

The audience members were polled as they left the Sofitel, with 39% saying Wilson had won the debate, followed by Sandell on 25% and Pickering on 16%. Just 13% were undecided at the end of the night and only 7% picked Carroll.

It appears no matter what the premier has to say, many Victorians have stopped listening.

- Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

articles.title: Cosa prevede l’accordo con il Ruanda sui centri di rimpatrio
articles.summary: L’intesa annunciata da cinque paesi europei con Kigali non è stata ancora firmata, e i costi e i dettagli del progetto che dovrebbe partire nel 2027 sono riservati
articles.preview: Come previsto, il 16 novembre cinque paesi europei hanno annunciato di avere avviato dei negoziati con il Ruanda per costruire un centro per il rimpatrio (o hub per il rimpatrio) previsto dalle nuove norme dell’Unione europea. Nel centro saranno trasferite con la forza le persone straniere irregolari che sono state espulse da un paese dell’Unione, ma che non possono essere rimpatriate, perché non esistono accordi con i paesi di origine.
articles.body:
Come previsto, il 16 novembre cinque paesi europei hanno annunciato di avere avviato dei negoziati con il Ruanda per costruire un centro per il rimpatrio (o hub per il rimpatrio) previsto dalle nuove norme dell’Unione europea. Nel centro saranno trasferite con la forza le persone straniere irregolari che sono state espulse da un paese dell’Unione, ma che non possono essere rimpatriate, perché non esistono accordi con i paesi di origine.

Non è stata ancora firmata alcuna intesa formale, ma il cancelliere austriaco Christian Stocker e la prima ministra danese Mette Frederiksen – insieme a ministri di Austria, Germania, Grecia e Paesi Bassi e al ministro dell’interno ruandese Vincent Biruta – hanno deciso di rendere pubblica la notizia.

È stata convocata una conferenza stampa a Vienna in sui sono intervenuti i rappresentanti dei cinque paesi, che hanno parlato di un “partenariato” con il Ruanda. Il piano prevede l’avvio delle deportazioni il prossimo anno, anche se il Ruanda è accusato di varie violazioni dei diritti umani.

Ma Stocker ha definito il progetto un “cambio di paradigma storico”. La sua posizione è stata condivisa da Frederiksen, che ha sottolineato la posizione comune della maggior parte dei paesi europei a favore di una politica migratoria più restrittiva e che prevede più rimpatri e trasferimenti forzati in paesi non europei.

“Siamo pronti a passare a misure più concrete”, ha dichiarato Frederiksen, aggiungendo che l’obiettivo è eliminare gli incentivi alla “migrazione illegale”, mandando un messaggio: chi ha un progetto migratorio non è il benvenuto in Europa.

Il ministro dell’interno ruandese Vincent Biruta ha dichiarato che chi arriverà in Ruanda potrà scegliere se rimanere con un permesso di soggiorno, tornare nel proprio paese d’origine o trasferirsi altrove. E ha ricordato l’esperienza con l’Organizzazione internazionale per le migrazioni (Oim) nei trasferimenti forzati dalla Libia verso un centro di transito in Ruanda, in attesa di un successivo reinsediamento altrove.

Nessuna informazione sui costi

I dettagli dell’operazione e dei negoziati che sono ancora in corso rimangono riservati. Messi sotto pressione dalle domande dei giornalisti durante la conferenza stampa, i rappresentanti dei cinque paesi europei non hanno fatto una stima di quanto costerà la costruzione di questi centri. Secondo alcune indiscrezioni potrebbe essere usata un edificio ristrutturato per un progetto simile del Regno Unito, il famigerato Hope hostel di Kigali.

I paesi europei sosterranno l’intero costo del trasferimento dei migranti e della loro permanenza in Ruanda. Al momento non è chiaro neanche cosa otterrà in cambio Kigali. Il governo ruandese, tuttavia, la prossima settimana firmerà un accordo di partenariato con la Danimarca sulla cooperazione in materia di migrazione.

Il centro ruandese dovrebbe funzionare inizialmente come progetto pilota, con una capienza di circa cento persone, una ventina per ciascun paese partecipante. Non dovrebbe essere un centro di detenzione: secondo quanto annunciato dai governi, le persone trasferite potranno circolare liberamente nel territorio ruandese.

Il progetto riguarderà persone adulte che hanno ricevuto un provvedimento di rimpatrio esecutivo e non possono essere ricondotte nel paese d’origine, per esempio perché le autorità di quello stato non collaborano. I minori dovrebbero essere esclusi dalla prima fase del progetto.

Contro le leggi fondamentali

Come è già avvenuto in passato per progetti simili, il piano solleva molti dubbi sul rispetto dei diritti umani, sui costi e sulla fattibilità. Human rights watch ha definito il progetto un “allontanamento particolarmente crudele” dai principi fondativi dell’Unione europea.

L’ong ha ricordato le violazioni documentate nel paese governato da Paul Kagame: repressione del dissenso, arresti arbitrari, maltrattamenti nelle carceri e intimidazioni ad attivisti e difensori dei diritti umani. Inoltre ha denunciato il sostegno militare ruandese al gruppo armato M23, responsabile di gravi violenze nella Repubblica Democratica del Congo.

I dubbi non riguardano solo le condizioni di accoglienza in Ruanda. Il trasferimento in un paese terzo potrebbe esporre le persone al rischio di essere successivamente rimandate in luoghi in cui sono in pericolo, senza che le autorità europee possano garantire un controllo effettivo sulle procedure.

Human rights watch sottolinea che i governi coinvolti restano vincolati alla Carta dei diritti fondamentali dell’Unione europea e alla Convenzione europea dei diritti umani. Il regolamento europeo sui rimpatri, inoltre, prevede che gli accordi possano essere conclusi solo con paesi che rispettano gli standard internazionali in materia di diritti.

“Gli stati dell’Unione possono chiamarli ‘centri di rimpatrio’ o perfino ‘centri di accoglienza’, ma nessun eufemismo può nascondere la violenza che deriva dallo sradicare le persone dalla vita che hanno costruito in Europa, per inviarle in un paese che non conoscono affatto, dove non hanno legami familiari, reti di supporto o prospettive concrete. Nessuna garanzia può cancellare una violenza di questo tipo”, ha commentato Chiara Catelli, portavoce di Picum, una rete di organizzazioni che si occupano di diritti umani.

“Al contrario, c’è da aspettarsi che queste persone vadano incontro a miseria, sfruttamento e, potenzialmente, a una catena di espulsioni. Senza contare che, com’è comprensibile, cercheranno di spostarsi di nuovo – per ricongiungersi a familiari e amici o per fuggire da un luogo che non hanno mai scelto – finendo magari per dover ricorrere a reti di trafficanti”, conclude Catelli.

Anche il precedente britannico pesa sulla discussione. Nel 2022 il governo di Londra aveva raggiunto un accordo con Kigali per trasferire in Ruanda persone arrivate nel Regno Unito in cerca di asilo. Ma il progetto è stato bloccato nel 2023, dopo che la corte suprema britannica lo ha giudicato illegittimo.

I giudici hanno riconosciuto il rischio che le persone trasferite potessero essere successivamente rimandate nei paesi da cui erano fuggite, esponendole a persecuzioni e trattamenti inumani sulla base di casi già documentati di richiedenti asilo e rifugiati trasferiti in Ruanda da Israele. Il governo britannico ha poi abbandonato il piano dopo aver speso centinaia di milioni di sterline.

L’Alto commissariato delle Nazioni Unite per i rifugiati (Unhcr) ha ricordato che qualsiasi iniziativa di questo tipo deve rispettare il diritto internazionale. Anche l’Organizzazione internazionale per le migrazioni (Oim) ha indicato che un suo eventuale coinvolgimento richiederà delle garanzie adeguate.

L’iniziativa non raccoglie il consenso di tutti i governi europei. La Francia è contraria alla creazione di centri di rimpatrio esterni all’Unione, mentre l’Italia si è tenuta fuori perché deve ancora affrontare il fallimento del suo progetto di realizzare dei centri in Albania, anche se la presidente del consiglio Meloni si è detta favorevole all’approccio.

[Il progetto di Roma e Tirana](http://Tutte le criticità dei nuovi centri di espulsione in Albania), nato per trasferire in Albania persone intercettate in mare e sottoporle a procedure d’asilo accelerate, è diverso da quello annunciato a Vienna, che riguarda invece persone già destinatarie di un provvedimento di rimpatrio.

Per ora, il numero delle persone coinvolte nel piano dell’accordo annunciato con il Ruanda sarà limitato. Ma la portata dell’iniziativa è soprattutto politica: normalizzare il trasferimento forzato di persone migranti fuori dai confini europei ed esternalizzare tutte le fasi delle procedure migratorie dalla gestione delle frontiere all’asilo, fino alle espulsioni. ◆

Typically, Phnom Penh's OCIC Wedding Hall hosts grand Khmer weddings. Yet on Monday, November 16, a major disagreement played out there, overshadowing the 20th summit of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), an organization gathering French-speaking countries. The OIF's 53 member states were unable to agree on the appointment of a new secretary-general, having failed to find a successor to Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda, and delegates left the venue three hours later than scheduled. This was a first in the organization's history.

Lacking a consensus, the summit's Cambodian presidency invited the gathered national leaders or their representatives to vote, by a show of hands, on a compromise measure. Their decision, which passed by 37 votes, postponed the election of the new leader by one year, with Mushikiwabo, who has held the position since 2018, set to remain in office during this period, in order to oversee a reform of the rules that govern appointing a secretary-general and prepare for an extraordinary summit.

According to several concurring sources, the incumbent secretary-general pledged not to run for a third term in office, and her country, Rwanda, agreed not to submit any other candidate. However, the candidacies of Coumba Bâ, from Mauritania, and Dacian Cioloș, from Romania, are said to remain in contention. The candidacy of Juliana Amato Lumumba, from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is also maintained "in its current state, unless evaluated otherwise," according to Congolese Communications Minister Patrick Muyaya, who spoke to Le Monde. New candidates will also be allowed to come forward.

articles.title: Nvidia partner Megaspeed being investigated by US government over chip exports
articles.summary: The Singapore-based company is suspected of helping to ship high-end AI chips from tech giant Nvidia to China, violating US export rules.
articles.preview: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China. In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024. It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
articles.body:
US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

articles.title: Why is a South China Sea Code of Conduct still unfinished after decades of talks?
articles.summary: Singapore is set to inherit negotiations for the long-delayed South China Sea Code of Conduct in 2027, with some of the toughest issues still unresolved.
articles.preview: Singapore is set to inherit negotiations for the long-delayed South China Sea Code of Conduct in 2027, with some of the toughest issues still unresolved. SINGAPORE: After decades of efforts to establish rules for managing disputes in the South China Sea, ASEAN and China have yet to conclude negotiations on a code of conduct for the heavily contested waterway.
articles.body:
Singapore is set to inherit negotiations for the long-delayed South China Sea Code of Conduct in 2027, with some of the toughest issues still unresolved.

SINGAPORE: After decades of efforts to establish rules for managing disputes in the South China Sea, ASEAN and China have yet to conclude negotiations on a code of conduct for the heavily contested waterway.

On Sunday (Nov 15), the first day of the ASEAN Leaders’ Summit in Manila, Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said about 80 per cent of the negotiating text had been provisionally agreed, but acknowledged that there was “no conclusion yet”.

Differing positions among ASEAN member states and China, as well as the time needed for negotiations, had prevented the agreement from being finalised this year, she said.

Experts CNA spoke to pointed to major sticking points, including the code’s geographical scope and whether it would be legally binding, that have proved difficult to overcome.

“There must be trust between the Southeast Asian claimants and China,” said Dr Ian Storey, principal fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute. “In the case of the Philippines and China, the trust deficit has widened over the past few years.”

The Philippines had made concluding the negotiations a priority of its ASEAN chairmanship. The task will now pass to Singapore when it takes over the bloc’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

CNA looks at why an agreement has proved so difficult to reach, what remains unresolved and whether a completed code would actually change behaviour in the South China Sea.

WHAT IS THE CODE OF CONDUCT?

The Code of Conduct is intended to establish rules to manage tensions in the disputed South China Sea, where Beijing's expansive maritime claims overlap with those of several Southeast Asian nations.

Efforts to draw up such a code date back to the 1995 ASEAN meetings that sought to manage overlapping maritime disputes in the South China Sea, said Gregory Poling from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

“It was not going to divide up the islands, but to set rules of the road that everybody could agree to,” said Poling, director and senior fellow of the Southeast Asia Programme and Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at CSIS.

However, negotiations hit a wall after ASEAN internally agreed on a draft in 1998, which it presented to China, he added.

“It was why they had to settle for the non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC). And ASEAN’s position was always that it should immediately lead to negotiations on the Code of Conduct, and the DOC was supposed to be an interim measure.”

More than two decades later, confrontations continue in the South China Sea.

The Philippines and China have repeatedly clashed in the waterway. Manila has accused Beijing of repeated aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, the use of water cannons and disrupting resupply missions. Meanwhile, China has accused the Philippines of intruding into what it claims as its territory.

Other ASEAN countries, namely Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei, also have overlapping claims with China. While Indonesia is not a claimant state, its North Natuna waters, which lie on the edge of the South China Sea, have also seen clashes between the Indonesian coast guard and Chinese fishing boats.

WHY HAVE NEGOTIATIONS TAKEN SO LONG?

Lazaro said several key questions remained unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.

"The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are," she told reporters at the ASEAN Summit on Sunday.

Experts told CNA that another fundamental obstacle is the code’s geographical scope: The parties have yet to agree on precisely where its rules would apply.

“The issue here has always been that even if you agree on a certain geographical scope, then as one of the parties, do you therefore essentially give de facto recognition to the other parties' claims?” said Dr Collin Koh from Nanyang Technological University’s S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).

For example, China does not want the Paracel islands to be included in the code’s geographical scope, while Vietnam does. Also known as Hoang Sa in Vietnamese, the Paracel islands are controlled by Beijing but have been claimed by Vietnam.

Beijing’s expansive claim in the South China Sea creates further complications because it overlaps with the exclusive economic zones of several Southeast Asian states.

Koh said ASEAN countries would have to consider whether accepting a geographical scope based on China’s claimed boundary could be interpreted as implicitly recognising Beijing’s claim.

"If China wants the geographical scope to cover well within the so-called 10-dash line, and if from the ASEAN perspective, you accept that, then does it mean that you essentially recognise that China does have a legitimate 10-dash line claim to it," he said.

Poling added that China would want to include areas within its claim, including waters off Malaysia and farther south that overlap with Indonesia’s waters.

“So there’s the whole bucket of, ‘How do we have a code if we can’t even agree on where we’re talking about?’” he said. “You can’t manage disputes if we can’t decide on where they are.”

Another major question is whether the eventual agreement would be legally binding.

Poling said that China’s preference would be for a code that is not legally binding.

Negotiators must also agree on what behaviour the code would seek to restrict.

RSIS’s Koh said the parties would have to define what constitutes a provocative action or conduct that goes against “the spirit of self-restraint”. This topic, he said, would be “contentious”.

“You need to define what exactly are those actions that go against the spirit of self-restraint … and the whole question of whether your actions are deemed provocative,” he explained.

“Essentially, it goes back to the 2002 (DOC), which does not essentially address these points so concisely, it just leaves it open-ended,” said Koh, adding that the open-endedness leaves it “very much open to everyone’s interpretation”.

COULD A DEAL BE REACHED NEXT YEAR?

The Philippines had made concluding the negotiations by the end of 2026 a key priority of its ASEAN chairmanship.

Lazaro said Manila had made substantial progress, with the proportion of provisionally agreed text rising from about 50 per cent to 80 per cent.

She had also expressed confidence that Singapore, which takes over the bloc’s chairmanship in 2027, “will be able to finish discussions next year”.

Analysts, however, cautioned that the 80 per cent figure did not necessarily mean an agreement was close.

“The last 20 per cent are the parts that matter,” Poling said.

“This is true of any negotiation, the hard part is the last part. Saying you’re 80 per cent done means you have done the easy things,” he said, adding that many of the same issues holding up the code today had also prevented progress in the late 1990s.

Storey, meanwhile, said three main obstacles would have to be overcome for an agreement to be reached.

“All the parties must be willing to compromise, and ASEAN must forge a consensus among the member states on the outstanding issues,” he said.

Trust would also be needed between China and the Southeast Asian claimant states, he said.

“Even though Singapore is a skilled diplomatic operator, forging a consensus within ASEAN and between ASEAN and China is going to be a very tough challenge.

“But hopefully Singapore will be up to the task and this time next year we’ll have a comprehensive, substantive and legally-binding (Code of Conduct),” said Storey.

Koh said much of the text agreed so far was “likely the tidying up of repetitive language on practical security cooperation measures”.

The remaining 20 per cent could include more difficult confidence- and security-building measures, as well as clauses “that will truly make a difference in promoting real peace and stability in the South China Sea”, he said.

“I suspect (these) are also the sort of prerequisite conditions that you need to create before you can even embark on practical security measures … I don’t think it necessarily means that we are any closer to getting the code.”

WOULD A CODE ACTUALLY CHANGE BEHAVIOUR IN THE SOUTH CHINA SEA?

Lazaro said negotiators had reached provisional agreement on how the existing 2002 DOC would relate to the proposed Code of Conduct.

Under the agreement, the declaration would provide the foundation for the new code, which would establish more substantive provisions to guide the conduct of parties in the waterway.

The parties have also agreed that the code would serve as a platform for practical maritime cooperation and a mechanism to manage differences at sea, rather than settle competing territorial claims.

But analysts cautioned that the conclusion of a code of conduct would not necessarily lead to changes in behaviour in the disputed waters.

For the code to “add value” to the existing declaration, Storey said it would need to include a list of prohibited activities that “reduce tension-generating behaviours”.

These could include, for example, prohibiting the occupation of new features and reclaiming atolls or using law enforcement vessels and warships to harass other countries’ coast guard vessels, drilling rigs, survey ships and fishing boats, or deploying offensive weaponry to occupied features.

Poling said agreeing on the code’s geographical scope was crucial.

“If you don’t have the geographical code agreed upon, then it’s useless,” he said. “And if it’s not legally binding, then it’s no different from the 2002 Declaration of Conduct, which has not accomplished anything."

Koh similarly cautioned that if concluding the Code of Conduct became “just another tick in the box” for ASEAN and China, it could end up as another “piece of paper” like the 2002 declaration.

“The only difference is that this time around, the damage is likely, reputationally, going to be bigger on ASEAN compared to 2002.”

articles.body:
A former US Foreign Service officer ran a company that funded election adverts attacking Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour.

The anonymous X account Habibi UK branded opponents of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza “racists”, “hate marchers” and “anti-Semites”, singling out politicians, broadcasters and campaigners for online attacks.

A six-month investigation by the British publication Byline Times has now identified the person behind the account as Benjamin Tait, a 61-year-old former United States Foreign Service officer who went on to run a British energy research company.

The news website and newspaper said that since the initial part of its investigation was published on Thursday, the account has stopped posting.

The account, which joined what was then Twitter in April 2015, used a coronation portrait of Queen Elizabeth I as its profile picture, gave its location as “The Realm” and quoted a line attributed to the monarch in its bio: “If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.”

An analysis of nearly 300,000 X posts placed @habibi_uk at the centre of a network of 13 anonymous accounts. It found that Habibi UK had posted more than 42,000 times.

The investigation also documented campaigns against 12 public figures in Britain over 10 months. Among those targeted were former BBC presenter and professional footballer Gary Lineker, photographer and outgoing chairman of London’s Southbank Centre arts centre Misan Harriman, documentary filmmaker Louis Theroux, actor and television panellist Nadia Sawalha and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. All of them had spoken out against Israel’s actions against Palestinians.

Here is what we know:

Who is Benjamin Tait?

Tait, a British-American grandson of philosopher Bertrand Russell, graduated from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service in Washington, DC. According to his LinkedIn profile, which has now been taken down, Tait spent two years as a US Department of State officer overseas with experience in political-military diplomacy and “counterterrorism research”.

Tait and his wife ran Prospex Research for about three decades. It was a firm that produced energy market reports for clients, including banks, consultancies, government officials and law firms. Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones quoted Tait on energy markets. The company entered voluntary liquidation in September.

Tait was writing under the name Habibi by at least 2008 on Harry’s Place, a British political blog that began as a centre-left forum. His early posts focused on alleged “Islamist extremism”, including pieces about campaigner Ismail Patel and the Palestinian aid charity Interpal, according to the investigation.

What was Tait’s role in campaign against Jeremy Corbyn?

Before the United Kingdom’s 2019 general election, Tait was the sole director and controlling owner of MTCAE Ltd, according to Companies House records cited by the Byline Times. The company ran Mainstream, a campaign registered to spend money during the elections independently of a political party.

Mainstream was founded and chaired by Ian Austin, a former Labour MP who quit the party under Jeremy Corbyn and has served as Britain’s trade envoy to Israel under five prime ministers. Austin said the group was set up to oppose “extremism” on the far left and hard right. But the Byline Times found that the Facebook advertisements it examined all attacked the Labour Party, including one that portrayed Corbyn as a national security threat.

Electoral Commission returns showed the company spent £134,457 pounds ($171,715) on the campaign, including 6,880 pounds ($8,786) paid to Tait for overhead costs and administration. The returns listed no donor.

Who amplified Habibi UK’s posts?

In March 2021, a High Court official ordered Twitter to disclose details behind the account to Professor David Miller, who had brought a legal claim. The operator’s name remained out of the public record. Despite this, the account went on to gain influence, particularly after Elon Musk took over Twitter in October 2022.

Links between the account and the Labour Party establishment run deep, according to the investigation. Austin, who is connected to Tait via Mainstream, shared posts from Habibi UK at least 34 times. John Woodcock, a former Labour MP who sits in the House of Lords, amplified the account 32 times, according to the investigation. It also found that David Toube, general counsel at the Jewish Leadership Council, amplified its posts hundreds of times.

The Henry Jackson Society, a British foreign policy think tank, cited Habibi UK nine times in a 2022 report on Hindu-Muslim unrest in Leicester.

articles.title: Miniere di possibilità e rischi
articles.summary: In Africa circa 13 milioni di persone lavorano nel settore senza autorizzazioni formali. Le loro condizioni sono precarie e molto pericolose

Questo territorio ha importanti riserve aurifere e nel corso degli anni ha attirato molti minatori artigianali anche dall’estero, soprattutto da Mali e Burkina Faso.
articles.body:
All’inizio di novembre, in un giro di vite contro le attività minerarie illegali, le autorità della Guinea hanno lanciato un’operazione su ampia scala per espellere decine di migliaia di cercatori d’oro stranieri che lavoravano senza autorizzazione nella regione di Siguiri, nel nordest del paese, vicino al confine con il Mali. Questo territorio ha importanti riserve aurifere e nel corso degli anni ha attirato molti minatori artigianali anche dall’estero, soprattutto da Mali e Burkina Faso.

Secondo le autorità del Mali, dove si sono riversati in massa questi lavoratori, gli espulsi sono stati circa 160mila, e i governi di Bamako e di Ouagadougou hanno dovuto organizzare in tutta fretta dei trasferimenti in camion per riportarli a casa. Ma le persone allontanate dalla Guinea – tra cui ci sono anche togolesi, beninesi e ivoriani – potrebbero essere anche il doppio, scrive Jeune Afrique, che prevede una crisi umanitaria, visto che molti sono rimasti senza alloggio e mezzi di sussistenza.

L’11 novembre a Siguiri sono scoppiati anche violenti scontri tra, da una parte, i minatori informali e gli abitanti del posto che protestavano contro le nuove restrizioni e, dall’altra, le forze di sicurezza. In tutto sono morte una decina di persone. Intanto nella città di Kankan sono state emesse le prime 194 condanne di minatori informali guineani e stranieri, ritenuti colpevoli di aver svolto attività illegali. Il governo afferma di voler prendere più saldamente il controllo del settore minerario e di voler tutelare l’ambiente, fa notare su Rfi Abdoul Sacko, attivista del Forum delle forze sociali della Guinea, ma non ha preparato bene il terreno, perché molte persone che vivono e lavorano nell’area di Siguiri non hanno alternative economiche. Si calcola che in questa regione centinaia di migliaia di persone, non solo straniere, dipendano dall’estrazione illegale di minerali.

Criminalizzazione

Dal Sudafrica al Ghana, dalla Repubblica Democratica del Congo allo Zambia, le attività minerarie informali danno da lavorare a circa 13,2 milioni di persone. Si calcola inoltre che questo settore sia il secondo o il terzo a impiegare più manovalanza dopo l’agricoltura e il commercio al dettaglio. Le condizioni di lavoro, oltre che precarie, sono molto pericolose, non solo per i rischi legati alle attività quotidiane, ma anche per la possibile presenza di organizzazioni criminali e gruppi armati in questi siti minerari, che sono controllati dai soggetti più vari. Infine ci sono anche i tentativi di criminalizzare questo tipo di lavoro, ricorda una recente analisi dell’Institute for security studies (Iss) di Pretoria, in Sudafrica.

Gli autori, Titilope F. Ajayi e Oluwole Ojewale, partono dal caso di 37 minatori artigianali, tra cui 14 minori (un ragazzo aveva solo 11 anni), che lo scorso settembre sono morti per asfissia mentre erano in custodia delle forze di sicurezza a Minna, nella Nigeria centrosettentrionale. La tragedia aveva scatenato molta indignazione nel paese. Le vittime facevano parte di un gruppo di una settantina di persone che erano state arrestate con l’accusa di svolgere attività illegali da un’unità speciale dedicata alle miniere dei Corpi di sicurezza e difesa civile nigeriani, una formazione paramilitare che risponde al ministero dell’interno.

Quelle decine di persone erano state rinchiuse per ore in una cella sovraffollata, troppo calda e senza un’adeguata ventilazione, e in 37 erano morti. Poche settimane fa una commissione d’inchiesta nigeriana ha stabilito che questi decessi si potevano evitare e che le condizioni di detenzione erano disumane.

Due anni fa aveva fatto invece molto scalpore in Sudafrica il caso di centinaia di minatori informali, i cosiddetti zama-zama, che erano rimasti intrappolati sottoterra ed erano morti in vecchie miniere abbandonate, dopo che le forze di polizia, per stanarli, si erano schierate intorno ai pozzi da cui si calavano sottoterra.

Nonostante questi abusi, il settore minerario informale continua a crescere, stima l’Iss, anche per la grande richiesta di queste materie prime. Nella sola Repubblica Centrafricana, per esempio, ci sono 2,6 milioni di minatori artigianali, in aumento di oltre il 2.500 per cento rispetto ai centomila del 2013. A trainare questa crescita è “la crescente domanda di risorse minerarie in un contesto di prezzi elevati delle materie prime”.

“In tutta l’Africa l’estrazione mineraria su piccola scala rappresenta una quota sostanziale della produzione mineraria, con un valore annuo in valuta estera compreso tra i 3 e i 5 miliardi di dollari statunitensi. Nel 2022 ha rappresentato una quota compresa tra il 32 e il 41 per cento della produzione totale di oro in Africa, mentre tra il 2017 e il 2023 ha coperto una percentuale tra il 52 e il 74 per cento della produzione globale di tantalio”, scrive l’Iss.

Nonostante tutti i pericoli, in un contesto di disoccupazione giovanile e di scarsi livelli d’istruzione è evidente che diventare minatori artigianali è ancora un’opzione attraente per i giovani africani che non hanno altre opportunità. “Molti di loro sono spinti dalla povertà. Criminalizzarli significa esporli ancora di più allo sfruttamento”, scrivono Ajayi e Ojewale. “Le autorità dovrebbero riconoscerli piuttosto come partner nelle economie estrattive, anche attraverso leggi che li proteggano dalle violazioni dei diritti umani. Inoltre dovrebbero espandere le opportunità di lavoro per i giovani, per ridurre il reclutamento nei conflitti armati e la dipendenza dallo sfruttamento minerario”.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Africana.

articles.title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine says the attack took weeks to plan, while the Kremlin vows to rebuild the strategic bridge.
articles.preview: Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort. articles.body:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the attack, though he is yet to comment.

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The Security Service of Ukraine said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.body:
Morning opening: Ukraine hits crucial bridge linking Russia and Crimea

Jakub Krupa

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.

The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.

The overnight strike followed an intensification of Russian attacks in the past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.

Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.

Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.

They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.

It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Slovakia planning to continue 'consultations' with Russia, despite Ukraine war

Meanwhile, Slovakia looks set to host another round of governmental consultations with Russia in 2027, foreign ministry documents scrutinised by Reuters showed, continuing the direct talks held last month for the first time since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.

The latest round of talks in October centred on discussions over Russian energy supplies, as well as culture and agriculture, and resumed a process suspended in 2022, Reuters noted.

Slovakia’s prime minister Robert Fico is a fairly regular guest in Moscow and has often faced criticism for his pro-Russian views and repeated call for engagement with Moscow, despite the continuing invasion of Ukraine.

Serbia's new deputies take seats in parliament after landmark Student List win

Guy de Launey

in Belgrade

The 140 successful candidates from Serbia’s Student List have just been sworn in as MPs at the National Assembly in Belgrade. They took the oath en masse, alongside members of the long-governing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which now finds itself in opposition for the first time in 14 years.

It follows the spectacular triumph of the Student List in last month’s parliamentary elections. It comfortably defeated the SNS and its populist leader Aleksandar Vučić with a slate of candidates drawn from academia, athletics and economics, among other disciplines. None of the new MPs have any political experience.

Before the parliamentary session, Student List supporters gathered outside the National Assembly to cheer their representatives. Some of them performed the traditional kolo circle dance in celebration.

Meanwhile, there were jeers and whistles for arrivals from Vučić’s party. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over the head of SNS candidate Lidija Vukićević, who said she felt “very bad” about the “primitivism and vulgarity” of Student List supporters.

Now the MPs have been sworn in, the next task is to elect a parliamentary speaker. Whoever it is become the acting president of Serbia – because Vučić resigned as head of state to make his unsuccessful attempt to become prime minister.

Biden's memoir uncovers his views on Zelenskyy, Ukraine, Macron, Brexit

Jakub Krupa

Separately, former US president Joe Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, got published today, and it features some interesting lines on European affairs.

Just skimming the book for now, there is a bit of interesting background on the US response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and his secret visit to Kyiv in February 2023, as well as some of Biden’s unfiltered views on Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“But I must admit that it could be difficult to work with Zelensky[y]. As brave as he and the Ukrainians were, they tested our patience on many occasions, demanding more armaments and money. …

Zelensky[y] could be moody and stubborn in our private conversations, and not as grateful as I would have expected. That could be frustrating, and I let him know that in no uncertain terms. Still, I refused to cut and run on the Ukrainians, who possessed a tremendous fighting spirit. And so did Zelensky[y].”

In longer paragraphs on Ukraine, Biden writes he was “not blind to Ukraine’s faults,”including “too much corruption” in the country’s judicial system, “where the rich and powerful were often free to buy their way out of accountability.” “Ukraine would have to deal with these challenges if they wanted genuine integration with Europe and the West.”

“But I had also seen the inner strength of the Ukrainian people.They deserved a fighting chance. If they could create a real democracy, with checks and balances, and fair elections, they could be a bulwark in the region, and an inspiration to peoples everywhere who were trying to claw their way out of a history of repression.”

He also reveals that Donald Trump’s transition team after the 2024 elections wanted to get a permission to immediately start negotiations with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

“During the transition, Donald Trump’s team had asked me to sign a letter empowering them to negotiate directly with Putin, even before he took office. But I refused, unwilling to give them carte blanche for what I expected would be a kind of surrender, at Ukraine’s expense.”

Elsewhere, Biden also writes about his relationships with other leaders, including first foreign trip as president, to attend a G7 summit in Cornwall in 2021, noting his “bittersweet” feelings about “saying goodbye to an old friend, Angela Merkel,” while remarking how “impressed” he was by France’s Emmanuel Macron.

“[He] enthusiastically welcomed me into the group, but he asked hard questions about the rise of populism in the United States and how it might affect our long-term foreign policy.”

“When I said, ‘America’s back,’ he responded, ‘For how long?’”

Writing about Brexit, Biden – who is of Irish heritage on his mother’s side – expresses his frustration that the withdrawal from the EU was “threatening to undermine the Good Friday agreement of 1998, which had done so much good in bringing peace to Northern Ireland.”

“I also disapproved of Brexit for its ultranationalist claims, and for making many promises that could not possibly be kept. I believed that the populist leaders and opportunists who backed Brexit had sold the British people a false bill of goods.”

Thursday's Ukraine talks 'very important' to get structure of peace negotiations right, Stubb says

Finland’s Alexander Stubb just addressed reporters in Berlin, after meeting Germany’s president Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Stubb said the upcoming meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday will be “very important” for the peace process.

“I think it’s important that we get a structure and order in the negotiations, which basically means that there’s a clear timetable and that there’s a clear agenda.”

He added:

“The process is not going to be fast, but I think it should be well structured. … I think the key here is that you cannot speak about territory without Ukraine. You cannot speak about security without Europe.”

Stubb also explained his approach to engagement with Russia, rooted in three key issues: geography, diplomacy and military.

“We need diplomacy. If you don’t talk about peace, you will never get peace. And in order to be able to get peace, you need to have dialogue and conversation and diplomacy. … We believe that in order for you to have a diplomatic say in the geographic situation that you are in, you have to back it up with something.”

Hungary suspends rail traffic to Ukraine after Russian drone hits railway station near border

Hungary will suspend rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days after a Russian drone struck just hundreds of meters from a railway station in western Ukraine, Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar said.

In a post on Facebook, Magyar said:

“Recently, in Transcarpathia, a Russian drone struck 300 meters from the Mukachevo railway station.

The Hungarian crew of the train arriving from Hungary has been taken off the train.

We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for today and tomorrow.”

Hungary’s foreign minister Anita Orbán – no link with that Orbán – offered a bit more detail on the incident.

In a post on X, she said:

“At around 10am Hungarian time, Russian Geran-2 drones attacked Transcarpathia in three waves, primarily targeting the areas around Mukachevo and Uzhhorod.

Ukrainian air defence forces responded effectively and shot down several of the attacking drones. Unfortunately, reports have also come in of multiple drone strikes, and the extent of the damage is currently being assessed.

This is not the first air attack against Transcarpathia, and unfortunately it is unlikely to be the last. As Russia intensifies its attacks against Ukraine’s civilian population, we can expect further attacks of this kind against Transcarpathia as well, which until now has been relatively protected due to its geographical location.

Ukraine’s civilian population is likely to face the most difficult winter of the war so far. The electricity grid and district heating systems are already in critical condition, particularly in Kyiv, Kharkiv and southern Ukraine. Russia is expected to intensify its attacks on power generation. Without electricity, water supplies in cities are also disrupted, millions of people are left without heating and power, and everyday life becomes increasingly difficult.

I express my solidarity with the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia and with the entire Ukrainian people, who have now had to face the horrors of war every day for nearly five years and are making extraordinary efforts simply to get through daily life.”

France's Le Pen vows to repeal Macron's pension reform, bring down retirement age

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen vowed to repeal President Emmanuel Macron’s pension reform if she is elected next spring and bring down the retirement age to 60 to 62.

She also set out plans to create a fund worth €900bn ($990.54bn) to help fund pensions in the long term, she added. It would take a generation to build up the fund, she added.

Reuters noted that pensions are France’s largest public spending item, due to reach more than €430bn ($474bn) next year. Successive governments have struggled to contain costs without provoking fierce public opposition.

RN President Jordan Bardella has said the party wants to tighten the rules governing pension contribution periods and encourage employers to keep older workers in jobs for longer.

'Trust has been restored' after crisis talks to save Dutch coalition government, PM Jetten says

On Friday, we reported on crisis talks aimed at saving Rob Jetten’s three-party minority government in the Netherlands.

The crisis erupted late last week when lawmakers from D66 and the Christian Democrats brokered a deal with center-left opposition parties in parliament to pass a contentious tax package, angering the third coalition partner. AP reported.

But it looks like they have managed to agree on a new way forward, with Jetten announcing a fresh start for the coalition bitterly divided by last week’s tax plans.

“We realise that we have tested the patience of the entire nation, but we are also relieved that, following several days of constructive discussions within the Cabinet and the coalition, trust has been restored,” Jetten said. “In doing so, we have laid the foundation to continue working together in this current composition.”

Kremlin says Kerch bridge will be rebuilt 'even better' after Ukrainian strike

Meanwhile, the Kremlin said its bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia will be “even better” after it is rebuilt following a large-scale Ukrainian attack that caused significant damage.

“There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.

Germany's Merz hosts Finland's Stubb for discussions on Ukraine ahead of key talks on Thursday

Finland’s highly influential president Alexander Stubb has arrived in Berlin this morning for talks with Germany’s Friedrich Merz.

The pair meets just two days before the highly anticipated threeway talks between US president Donald Trump, China president Xi Jinping, and Russia president Vladimir Putin in Manila and an ‘unprecedented’ meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday.

The Berlin meeting is expected to bring together over 30 national leaders, including Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the two US peace envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who will be able to brief European partners on the Manila talks held a few hours earlier, Politico Berlin Playbook reported.

Zelenskyy hails 'unprecedented operation' that led to strike against Kerch Bridge

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has hailed the strike against the Kerch Bridge as “an unprecedented operation” with direct consequences “for the primary military supply route connecting Russian territory to our Ukrainian Crimea.”

He said it was “the seventh phase of an operation that has been under way for several weeks,” with “systematic” destruction of air defence systems, radar and other electronic warfare assets.

“We have repeatedly proposed de-escalation measures to Russia, yet every such proposal has been met only with emphatic rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure daily – including bridges – in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region.

We are restoring our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capacity is and will remain high, and we will never leave terror against our cities and our people unanswered.”

46 injured, four seriously, in train crash in Prague

I am also keeping an eye on an incident in the Czech capital of Prague where two commuter trains collided near the main train station, leaving 46 injured, including four seriously.

The two passenger trains collided on an overpass while travelling at a low speed around 7am this morning, according to the Czech media.

Czech transport minister called it “a very serious” incident, but said the focus was on caring for all affected.

At 10am Czech time, the city’s emergency services said the situation was contained, with all injured transported to hospitals.

'Europe needs to wake up' to realise defence costs if Ukraine fails, Danish minister says

Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus has warned that “Europe needs to wake up” as “the price, if Ukraine falls, will be lot higher than the amount we are now delivering for Ukraine.”

“Ukraine has the most efficient and also modern army in all of Europe. We are gaining a lot of advantages [from] the cooperation with the Ukrainians,” he said.

But he added that “the cost of Ukraine losing will be a lot higher” than any current aid given to Kyiv.

Germany to contribute $300m for US air defence systems for Ukraine ahead of 'exceptionally difficult winter', Pistorius says

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Ukraine is facing “an exceptionally difficult winter” amid intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure as he confirmed Germany will fund a new package of air defence systems for Kyiv.

“Ukraine is facing an exceptionally difficult winter as Russia is doing everything in its power - and will continue to do so – to destroy Ukraine’s water, electricity and energy infrastructure,” he said.

Pistorius said that Russia was “intensifying its aerial assaults because its if failing to make progress on the battlefields.”

“For us, as nations supporting Ukraine, this means one thing clearly: we must continue to provide effective and rapid support for Ukraine’s air defence,” he said.

Germany will contribute $300m for another round of defensive weapons purchases from the US, with Norway also expected to join.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is about far more than solidarity or assisting a nation under attack; it is about the security of Europe – and, by extension, about stopping Putin and keeping him in check.”

During the Ukraine defence contact group, which Pistorius co-chairs, the EU ministers will be joined by the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby.

“This is important, as we have several matters to discuss – for instance, the upcoming Force Posture Review, as well as cooperation on defence equipment and various other topics.”

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.

The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.

The overnight strike followed an intensification of Russian attacks in the past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.

Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.

Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.

They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.

It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Colpito il Ponte di Crimea, 'crollata un'arcata, parte della carreggiata in mare'
articles.summary: Il governo russo terrà una riunione sul "ripristino" del ponte dopo il secondo attacco in 24 ore all'infrastruttura. Kiev, i due ponti principali della città chiusi dopo gli attacchi russi
articles.preview: Uno degli archi del ponte di Crimea e una parte della sua carreggiata sono finiti in mare dopo il secondo attacco subito dall'infrastruttura e ora il traffico, sia ferroviario che stradale, sul ponte è stato sospeso. Lo scrive Ukrainska Pravda che cita come fonti il ministero dei Trasporti russo, oltre alla testata russa Astra e i canali Telegram ucraini Supernova+ ed Exilenova e Krymsky Veter ("Vento di Crimea"), un canale Telegram locale della Crimea.
articles.body:
Uno degli archi del ponte di Crimea e una parte della sua carreggiata sono finiti in mare dopo il secondo attacco subito dall'infrastruttura e ora il traffico, sia ferroviario che stradale, sul ponte è stato sospeso. Lo scrive Ukrainska Pravda che cita come fonti il ministero dei Trasporti russo, oltre alla testata russa Astra e i canali Telegram ucraini Supernova+ ed Exilenova e Krymsky Veter ("Vento di Crimea"), un canale Telegram locale della Crimea. Secondo il canale ucraino Exilenova+, si è trattato di un attacco combinato, portato a termine con missili FP-5 Flamingo.

Tuttavia, questa informazione non è stata ancora ufficialmente confermata.

Il canale Telegram Astra precisa che sono state attaccate due arcate del ponte, come il giorno precedente. Una di esse è stata distrutta. Secondo Krymsky Veter, è crollata anche una campata carrabile e il canale navigabile è disseminato di detriti. Il ministero dei Trasporti russo ha comunicato che, a seguito del secondo attacco di droni, il traffico sia sulla parte stradale che su quella ferroviaria del ponte è stato sospeso mentre i danni sono in fase di valutazione.

Il governo russo terrà una riunione sul "ripristino" del Ponte di Crimea presieduta dal vice primo ministro Marat Khusnullin, dopo il secondo attacco delle forze armate ucraine in 24 ore all'infrastruttura che collega la penisola annessa da Mosca nel 2014 alla costa del Mar Nero. Le autorità russe non hanno ancora fornito informazioni sulle conseguenze dell'attacco, ma media indipendenti hanno diffuso immagini delle arcate parzialmente crollate del ponte. "La riunione affronterà il tema del ripristino del Ponte di Crimea e dell'organizzazione dei collegamenti di trasporto", secondo una dichiarazione del governo citata da Interfax.

Quella condotta dalle forze ucraine in Crimea è una "operazione senza precedenti condotta in risposta agli attacchi russi contro le nostre infrastrutture". Lo scrive su Telegram il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky che ha ringraziato le forze armate e i servizi di sicurezza oltre che i produttori di armi del Paese. "Abbiamo ripetutamente offerto alla Russia misure di de-escalation e abbiamo ricevuto solo fermi rifiuti a tutte le proposte. La Russia colpisce quotidianamente le nostre infrastrutture, compresi i ponti, a Zaporizhia, Dnipro, Kiev e nella regione di Odessa" scrive Zelensky.

Il presidente ucraino ricorda "alla Russia che la guerra tornerà sempre al punto di partenza. Il potenziale di difesa dell'Ucraina è e sarà elevato, e non lasceremo mai impunito il terrorismo contro le nostre città e il nostro popolo". Il danneggiamento del ponte in Crimea "è il risultato della settima fase dell'operazione, durata diverse settimane, ideata e coordinata dal Servizio di Sicurezza insieme allo Stato Maggiore delle Forze Armate ucraine". Lo racconta il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky su Telegram.

"I nostri soldati hanno gradualmente distrutto sistemi di difesa aerea, radar, apparecchiature di guerra elettronica e altri obiettivi designati, nel percorso verso il traguardo finale. A tal fine, sono stati impiegati i sistemi Dovbush, Vendetta, Da Vinci, Sichen, MICH 2000, Ruta, Palanytsia, An-197, FP-1, FP-5 Flamingo e R-360 Neptune" scrive. "Oggi - già in una fase cruciale - i droni 'Palyanytsia', che hanno colpito la parte carrabile del ponte, e i missili 'Neptun', i droni 'Ruta' e FP-5, che hanno colpito la parte ferroviaria, si sono dimostrati esemplari. Con l'aiuto del 'Flamingo' i nostri soldati hanno condotto una sconfitta controllata - e le comunicazioni hanno funzionato perfettamente fino agli ultimi secondi" aggiunge.

Guerra agli snodi cruciali, colpiti due ponti a Kiev, gli ucraini attaccano il ponte di Crimea

Gli attacchi russi hanno colpito in tarda serata due importanti ponti a Kiev. Lo ha reso noto il sindaco della capitale ucraina Vitaly Klitschko, poco dopo che l'aeronautica militare ucraina aveva lanciato un allarme per l'arrivo di missili. "Secondo le prime informazioni, sono stati colpiti i ponti Nord e Sud della capitale", ha scritto Klitschko in un post su Telegram. "A seguito dell'attacco nemico, sono state danneggiate infrastrutture critiche. In alcuni quartieri si registrano interruzioni nell'erogazione di acqua e riscaldamento", ha aggiunto.

Attacco a un importante impianto petrolifero Gazprom in Russia, scoppiato un incendio

Nella notte è scoppiato un incendio in un importante complesso di raffinazione petrolifera e petrolchimico nella Repubblica di Baschiria, in Russia, in concomitanza con notizie di un attacco di droni nella regione, stando a quanto riporta il Kyiv Independent. Alcuni canali Telegram di monitoraggio ucraini hanno segnalato che il complesso Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat nella città di Salavat è stato preso di mira. Foto e video diffusi mostrano un grande bagliore proveniente da un incendio nei pressi dell'impianto industriale. Situato a circa 1.750 chilometri a est di Kiev, Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat è uno dei più grandi complessi petroliferi e petrolchimici della Russia, in grado di lavorare fino a 10 milioni di tonnellate di petrolio e condensato di gas all'anno. L'impianto produce benzina, gasolio e altri prodotti petroliferi e chimici. La struttura è stata ripetutamente bersaglio di attacchi di droni ucraini. Più recentemente, lo Stato Maggiore ucraino ha confermato un attacco al complesso avvenuto l'8 ottobre , che ha provocato un vasto incendio.

Filorussi, 'l'esercito ucraino ha colpito il ponte di Crimea, il traffico è bloccato'

Le forze armate ucraine hanno attaccato il ponte di Crimea e il traffico è bloccato fino a mezzogiorno, ha riferito il governatore della regione annessa dalla Federazione Russa nel 2014, Serghei Aksyonov. "Il nemico ha colpito il ponte di Crimea. Per questo motivo, il traffico sarà limitato fino a mezzogiorno circa. Sono stati dispiegati tutti i servizi necessari per far fronte all'emergenza ed è stato istituito un centro di risposta alle emergenze a Kerch", ha scritto Aksyonov su Telegram.
