articles.body:
Energy facilities, industrial units, ports and bridges, schools, hospitals and apartment buildings have already been hit in Iran and across the region.

Tehran, Iran – Iranians say they are concerned about United States media reports that civilian infrastructure could be hit if the US launches a new war on Iran.

The New York Times published an investigative report on Monday claiming some overlap between dam building in Iran and suspected underground missile sites, as well as military demand for water and electricity.

The report acknowledged that the connection remains speculative, but has received backlash for linking civilian infrastructure to the military.

Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, civilian infrastructure in Iran has been extensively damaged in air attacks, impacting energy supplies, logistics, and the economy.

Navid, a 34-year-old resident of Tehran who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that after his experiences in the war, “it’s worrying how easily conversations have shifted to talking about attacking fundamental things like water, electricity and gas.”

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the report was “preparing the next round” of attacks on civilian infrastructure.

“Cool. New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” read a post on his X account.

Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, CEO of the London-based Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, said fewer than 50 of Iran’s more than 500 large dams have turbines installed to generate electricity.

“The reason there are so many dams in Iran is because there are vested interests, including IRGC construction companies, that use infrastructure budgets to generate rents,” he explained on X.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, also highlighted “recent acts of aggression by the USrael [sic] against Iran, water storage reservoirs”.

“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” he wrote on X.

Deep concerns

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to destroy Iranian power plants and bridges in the event of a new war and said he was “not at all” concerned that such attacks could constitute war crimes. Last week, Trump said all key infrastructure in Iran could be “wiped out” in three days, beginning with bridges. Trump has also warned that US forces are “fully locked and loaded” and have 38 bridges in their crosshairs.

The US has already been strongly criticised by Tehran for bombing a girls’ school in Minab on the first day of the war, killing 120 children.

Airwars, a United Kingdom-based nonprofit that tracks civilian harm in conflict-affected nations, documented almost 1,000 “incidents of harm”, where at least one person was killed in acts of violence across the Middle East, during the first 40 days of the war.

US-based rights groups in April, during the height of the war, reported that 1,701 civilians had been killed in the US-Israel assault on Iran, including at least 254 children.

Given their experiences during the war, Iranians have been concerned about the prospect of more civilian sites being targeted.

Mostafa Najafi, a political analyst close to the security establishment, also believes the “targeted and inhumane” media report seeks to normalise attacks on civilian targets, which could undermine social stability in Iran.

“By turning an unverified coincidence in timing and geographical overlap into a security hypothesis, this report has laid the groundwork for suggesting that some of Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including water-transfer projects, forms part of a military support network,” he wrote in a social media post.

“Undoubtedly, this narrative framework could influence future debates about the nature of military and civilian targets and the legitimacy of attacking Iran’s critical infrastructure.”

The Tasnim and Mehr news websites, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also similarly described the investigation as an engineered report intended to justify attacks.

A number of the experts quoted in the investigation said later they do not support attacks on civilian infrastructure, or the hypothesis that dams are directly supporting military projects.

“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” said Kaveh Madani, director of the UN University’s water institute, who is also a former deputy head of Iran’s Department of Environment.

“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles!” he wrote on X. “This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure”.

Civilian targets

During both the 12-day war of June 2025 and the current war starting on February 28, civilian infrastructure – often claimed to be “dual use” – has been widely targeted in air attacks.

Oil, gas and petrochemical facilities in southern Iran, oil depots across Tehran, a power plant in Khorramshahr, as well as a desalination plant in Qeshm and water reservoirs in Fars and Khuzestan have been attacked.

The B1 bridge in Karaj near Tehran, among the biggest in the Middle East, was extensively damaged just days before opening to traffic. Multiple bridges were destroyed in Bandar Khamir in southern Hormozgan, while the Bandar Abbas railway junction in the south and Aq Tekeh Khan railway bridge to the north were struck to create disruptions.

Steel and aluminium factories, airports, commercial ports and fishing infrastructure, hospitals and emergency services, medicines manufacturing and public-health research centres, apartment buildings, schools and universities were also among the targets.

Iran’s armed forces have launched missile and drone attacks at civilians and military sites across the Arab world, including the Ras Laffan LNG production facilities in Qatar, and refineries, airports and other facilities.

Iran’s leadership has promised it will pursue “maximum deterrence” through an unfettered response without geographical limits if the country is attacked again.

Despite ongoing mediated negotiations, Iran and the US continue to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, where the IRGC struck multiple vessels attempting “unauthorised” routes over the past day.

The IRGC also said it attacked a US radar system at Sheikh Isa Airbase in Bahrain on Tuesday in what it called a response to lingering US violations of Iranian airspace.

articles.title: Yemen's government forces withdraw from Bab al-Mandab and west coast to defend Aden
articles.summary: Yemen's government forces withdraw from Bab al-Mandab and west coast to defend Aden Submitted by MEE correspondent on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 09:43 Houthis advance in Lahij amid government withdrawal, reaching within 70km of provisional capital Armoured vehicles are left damaged near the sea as Saudi-backed forces sustain losses against Houthi forces, in a location given as near Bab el-Mandab, Yemen, in this screengrab from a handout video released 16 November 2026 (Ansar Allah Military Media/Handout via Reuters) On Early last month, the chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced the launch of Operation Fajr al- Yemen (Dawn of Yemen), aimed at restoring state institutions, retaking the capital, Sanaa, and ending Houthi control. The announcement came a day after the Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, seized large areas of Taiz governorate and took control of all entrances to Taiz city. However, no advances have been made on the ground since the operation was announced. Instead, the Houthis have continued to make major gains in both Taiz and Lahij governorates, in Yemen's southwest. On the west coast, battles were ongoing in Dhubab district, where government forces controlled the Dhubab military airport and surrounding areas. Meanwhile, the Houthis were advancing through the mountains and valleys of Lahij governorate and were on the verge of imposing a siege on military forces along the coast. On Sunday, 15 November, Yemeni government forces announced the withdrawal of their troops from the Bab al-Mandab area and Dhubab military airport as part of a redeployment aimed at securing the provisional capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates. The Houthis advanced into all the areas previously held by government forces on the same day. They are now roughly 70km from Aden's northern entrance, while government forces are regrouping to defend the city. The latest advance has given the Houthis control of approximately 60km of coastline along the Gulf of Aden, stretching from Bab al-Mandab towards Aden governorate, including the coastal area of Khour Omaira. Defending Aden Professor Abdulsattar al-Shamiri, a Yemeni political analyst and CEO of the Johood Center for Studies and Research, said the recent withdrawals should be viewed in the context of battlefield management. He pointed to a failure to close gaps early on, allowing the Houthis to outflank and besiege forces that had advanced towards Dhubab. “This reflects an inability to manage the battle and control the ground through collective management and coordination among all military units,” Shamiri told Middle East Eye. 'The Houthis may exploit their control over strategic areas to consolidate their influence in Bab al-Mandab while keeping the option of advancing toward Aden open' - Mansour al-Muntasir, political analyst Shamiri said this also exposed clear logistical shortcomings, including the failure to rapidly supply food and ammunition and to rescue small units stationed in the mountains, which are forced to withdraw when they run out of ammunition. “What happened is also the result of the failure in the Tur al-Baha military axis, which pulled out from vast areas in the countryside of Taiz,” he added. “The withdrawal caused confusion among the forces present on the west coast and other units that tried to fill the gap left by the collapse of the axis in southern rural Taiz and the districts of Tur al-Baha and al-Maqatirah in Lahij governorate. “I believe that government forces in and around Dhubab feared being outflanked by the Houthis and becoming exhausted in that location, so they chose to focus on defending Lahij and Aden specifically.” On the possibility of a Houthi advance towards Aden, Shamiri said the group might attempt to push further south, but that such an operation would be difficult, particularly given the air cover. “The matter is not impossible, but it will not be easy for them, and the probability of advancing toward Aden is very low now,” he said. At the same time, Shamiri said, reorganising the theatre of operations could allow government forces to launch offensives on other fronts and shift from a defensive to an offensive posture. The last time the Houthis seized Aden governorate was in 2015, at the beginning of the Yemeni civil war, before government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, recaptured it and advanced into neighbouring governorates, including Lahij. Bab al-Mandab is priority Professor Mansour al-Muntasir, a Yemeni political analyst, agrees with Shamiri that the developments in Dhubab and surrounding areas point to shortcomings in government military planning and diverging priorities among anti-Houthi forces. Most of the government forces that withdrew from the coast on Sunday come from southern governorates. This has led some southern activists to support the withdrawal, arguing that these troops should focus on defending the south against the Houthis, effectively leaving governorates north of Aden to the Houthis and northern fighters. 'The government's withdrawal reflects an inability to manage the battle and control the ground through coordination among all military units' - Abdulsattar al-Shamiri, political analyst However, Muntasir doesn’t believe that was the main reason behind the withdrawal. “I do not rule out that some southern forces may have preferred to focus on protecting Aden and the southern areas, but it is difficult to assert that this is the sole reason for the withdrawal,” Muntasir told MEE. While some believe the Houthis have gained popular support during their advances over the past two months in rural Taiz and parts of Lahij, Muntasir takes a different view: “I do not believe the Houthi advance is necessarily evidence of popular acceptance so much as a result of divisions and poor coordination among their adversaries.” At least three different groups are fighting the Houthis in Lahij governorate: al-Amaliqa (the Giants Brigades), the Nation’s Shield Forces, and the National Guard. While they operate under separate leaderships, all ultimately fall under the Ministry of Defence. With the Houthis now controlling all areas around Bab al-Mandab, Muntasir says they could leverage their position: “In my estimation, the Houthis may exploit their control over strategic areas to consolidate their influence in Bab al-Mandab while keeping the option of advancing toward Aden open. “The real danger is that the continued fragmentation of government and southern forces may grant them additional opportunities to expand.” More displaced families The International Organization for Migration reported that 347,321 people were displaced between 1 August and 14 November. Its report also recorded the displacement of 18,780 people, comprising 3,130 families, between 8 and 14 November. ‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma ees warned that nearly 9,600 displaced people face increasing risks as fighting draws closer to the Kharaz Refugee Camp in Lahij governorate. Humanitarian activist Abdulrahman al-Asadi, who has worked with several local aid organisations, says the humanitarian situation is deeply concerning, as hundreds of thousands of people have been forced to flee their homes by the fighting, with many losing both their residences and sources of livelihood. “The real challenge is not just in providing aid, but in delivering it to those who need it through humanitarian organisations, local partners, and field teams, as there are major obstacles, most notably ongoing clashes, road closures, insecurity, and difficulty accessing affected areas,” he told MEE. Before the latest escalation, Yemen already had 5.2 million internally displaced people, out of a total of 22.3 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, according to the 2026 Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. articles.body:
Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.

Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.

Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “No 1 terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost of living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.

Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon and public holidays put in place for the Asean summit.

After departing from Fairbanks in Alaska, Trump emerged from Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International airport at 5.54pm local time (0954 GMT), live video showed.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen in China on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ousting of the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump’s delegation was expected to include Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.

“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said. “Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.

“So, yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”

The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.

Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 100km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 26 participating signatory governments.

Amnesty International said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.

“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” Amnesty’s director for the Philippines, Ritz Lee Santos III, said. “Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.

“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective,” he wrote. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

Earlier, Russian forces struck two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone and missile attacks across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.

The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted on Telegram.

He added: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, after which one of the country’s deputy prime ministers, Marat Khusnullin, briefed Putin on the damage to the bridge, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.

Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.

But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.

“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

The Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.

He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”

Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on Fire”, a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.

Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.

The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.

Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.

Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.

Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway.

Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.

Russian forces launched a series of attacks on bridges crossing the river earlier this month and in October.

A Russian missile attack injured three people in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Tuesday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.

The ministry said the strikes also targeted energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels used by Ukraine’s armed forces.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.

Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner said progress had been made towards an agreement, though important challenges remain to end the war, which Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

articles.body:
La economía europea está mostrando más resistencia de la prevista a la crisis que ha provocado la guerra en Oriente Próximo como demuestra la mejora, casi generalizada, de las previsiones económicas de la Comisión Europea. Pronostica Bruselas que el producto interior bruto (PIB) de la zona euro crecerá un 1,2% este año, tres décimas por encima de los cálculos divulgados en primavera. La mejora prevista para el conjunto del área monetaria es, en todo caso, débil y el crecimiento sigue siendo escaso o “mediocre”, como lo definió el FMI el pasado octubre . Seguir leyendo

articles.title: ‘Will you stand watch with me?’ Israel cracks down on foreign activists in West Bank
articles.summary: ‘Will you stand watch with me?’ Israel cracks down on foreign activists in West Bank Submitted by Kate McMahon on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 14:54 As settler attacks intensify during the olive harvest, international volunteers face arrest, deportation and entry bans for accompanying Palestinians and documenting abuses A Palestinian farmer watches for Israeli settlers during the olive harvest in Turmus Ayya, northeast of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, on 20 October 2026 (Zain Jaafar/AFP) Off In Masafer Yatta, on the southern edge of the occupied West Bank, a mural stretches across a village guesthouse, posing a question: “Will you stand watch with me?” The question is directed at international volunteers arriving in the rural Palestinian community. But a recent escalation in Israeli crackdowns has meant less outside support. As settler violence against Palestinians intensifies during the annual olive harvest, Israeli authorities have stepped up measures against foreign activists, including bans and deportations. According to news reports and campaigners, more than 40 international activists have been deported since 1 October over allegations including entering a restricted zone, disrupting public order and terrorism. “Despite their obsessive and extensive surveillance apparatus, the occupation is afraid of people knowing the truth about what’s going on. Whenever we witnessed a settler attack, we were immediately ordered to stop filming by the army,” a German activist told Middle East Eye. The activist, who declined to be identified, was arrested on 6 November and subsequently deported. “They even took away people’s phones or destroyed them,” she added. 'The occupation is desperately trying to hide their crimes from the world' - German activist The rise in deportations has raised concerns that Israel is pursuing a new strategy to remove international observers from the West Bank, as high-profile settler attacks bring increasing international scrutiny of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and the military’s alleged cooperation with settlers. Meanwhile, foreign journalists and observers have been barred from entering the Gaza Strip for the past three years, except tightly controlled embeds with the Israeli army. Some fear similar restrictions on foreign access could take hold in the West Bank. “The occupation is desperately trying to hide their crimes from the world, which is why this year we have seen more international witnesses deported than ever before,” the German activist added. Long history of international activism Across the occupied West Bank, numerous groups recruit international volunteers to provide what they call a “protective presence”, leveraging their “passport privilege” to shield Palestinians from Israeli violence. By documenting human rights abuses and legal violations, and simply being physically present, activists hope their foreign passports will deter Israeli soldiers and settlers from attacking the Palestinians they accompany. Sometimes, the tactic works. During this year’s olive harvest season, hundreds of activists have accompanied Palestinians to their olive groves and assisted with the harvest. They pluck olives from dense branches, but they also watch astutely, scanning the hills for approaching settlers. Sometimes, they can provide an early warning system and enough time for people to flee. Throughout the rest of the year, volunteers take turns on night shifts in villages vulnerable to settler attacks, believing their presence makes assaults less likely. Rachel Corrie and Gaza brought back to the London stage  (ISM), founded in 2001 to organise popular resistance and bring international volunteers to Gaza and the West Bank. In an infamous 2003 incident, ISM activist Rachel Corrie was killed by an Israeli bulldozer while protesting housing demolitions in the Gaza Strip. Other groups have since emerged, including Faz3a, founded in 2019. Its stated mission is “to mobilise international volunteers under local Palestinian guidance to provide direct civil protection, reinforce Palestinian sumud (steadfastness), and build an international solidarity network.” Both groups advocate non-violence and deploy volunteers as a civilian protection force. But the strategy is becoming less effective as Israeli forces and settlers face little international accountability. In 2024, Israeli forces shot dead Turkish-American ISM volunteer Aysenur Ezgi Eygi as she sheltered behind an olive tree. No one has been charged over her killing. “Laws are empty promises when no one is enforcing them, and in order to do that, we need more international pressure,” the deported German activist said. Removing witnesses Israeli authorities have in recent years increased the detention and deportation of international activists, as settler violence reaches record levels . The crackdown intensified after outgoing National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir established a specialised police task force in 2024 to track, detain and deport international solidarity activists in the West Bank. During the 2025 olive harvest, 32 foreign activists with the Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC) were arrested en route to the harvest, deported and banned from entering Israel for 99 years. Israeli authorities subsequently raided the organisation’s headquarters, effectively shutting it down. 'We were there to pick olives, and we were doing nothing wrong and nothing illegal' - Council member in Italy's La Spezia Following the deportation of two Jewish-Americans in October 2025, Israeli police and the army issued a joint statement saying the Samaria District Police were acting under Ben Gvir’s policies to target foreign nationals involved in “incitement and provocations”. The deportations have accelerated during this year’s olive harvest. On 6 October, four ISM activists were detained in Jamma’in, in the Nablus Governorate, and deported. On 22 October, settlers in Masafer Yatta reportedly held 11 Faz3a volunteers at gunpoint before the military arrived and marked them for deportation. On 30 October, Israeli forces detained and deported 14 ISM volunteers from al-Lubban al-Gharbi, in the Ramallah and al-Bireh Governorate. On 6 November, authorities arrested 12 Faz3a activists, three Palestinians and two Italian journalists harvesting olives in Kafr Ni’ma, west of Ramallah. Settlers reportedly detained the group first, separating the Palestinians from the activists. The volunteers said Palestinian farmer Yaqoub, who owned the land, suffered two broken ribs in an assault by settlers. They said they heard his screams but could not see him. “We were abducted, first by armed settlers and then by the Israeli occupation army, and then deported and sent home. It was unjust and illegal. We were there to pick olives, and we were doing nothing wrong and nothing illegal,” Giorgia Lombardi, an activist and council member in La Spezia, Italy, told MEE. “For us, it was just two days in prison, and we had an embassy, a passport, and a flight home. It is nothing compared with what the Palestinian people have lived under for 80 years, every single day, with nowhere to go back to,” she added. 'The settlers are in control': How the West Bank is being ethnically cleansed ivists had been deported from Kafr Ni’ma for “violating legal provisions” and “disrupting public order”. Beyond the deportations, even more activists, the numbers of whom are not available, have recently been denied entry into Israel at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv and the King Hussein Bridge crossing with Jordan. Nina, an Italian activist who volunteered with Faz3a in 2025, was denied entry at Ben Gurion in November 2026. She said an immigration officer demanded access to her phone contacts and private WhatsApp messages. “I told him I was happy to show him my phone, but in Italy we have privacy rights. He told me: ‘Israel isn’t Italy. Where do you think you are?’ He said he was the one calling the shots,” she told MEE. “He went into my contacts without permission, and then he printed out an expulsion notice.” Israeli authorities also revoked the visa of former US Congresswoman Cori Bush while she was on her way to Tel Aviv earlier this month. Bush is an outspoken critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and visited the West Bank in September. Activists undeterred For now, the activists remain undeterred. In Ramallah, the West Bank’s administrative capital, 12 new volunteers have just arrived. 'We wish that for each deported person, a hundred will come in their place' - German activist They laugh and trade tales of cover stories they gave immigration officers to convince them they were tourists. Meanwhile, others gather around a phone to join a video call with their deported comrades. “If you have not lost something in this fight, you are not fighting hard enough yet. Those of us deported are only stronger,” said a Canadian activist. “In prison, we had privileges that Palestinians can only dream of.” “We wish that for each deported person, a hundred will come in their place,” said the German activist, speaking from Berlin. articles.title: Trump to raise Ukraine war in talks with Xi and Putin at APEC
articles.summary: The Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take place between the leaders of China, the US and Russia.
articles.preview: China The southern Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take center stage. President Donald Trump is preparing to sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday in an unprecedented three-way summit of the world's three largest nuclear powers, leaving US allies wondering where they stand.
articles.body:
China

The southern Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take center stage.

President Donald Trump is preparing to sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday in an unprecedented three-way summit of the world's three largest nuclear powers, leaving US allies wondering where they stand.

The significance of the gathering may have less to do with concrete agreements than with the message it sends about Trump's approach to the world's major powers, said Jonathan Czin, a former CIA China expert now at the Brookings Institution.

"What will be more important than the substance of this meeting is going to be the subtext," Czin said. He said US allies in Asia and Europe could see the Trump administration as more focused on accommodating China and Russia than countering their influence.

The meeting marks a striking departure from the strategy of Trump's first administration, when Washington identified China and Russia as its principal geopolitical competitors.

"We've gone 180 degrees from saying these are the main problems we face in the national security space for the US government, to now we're going to have a major meeting with these two leaders," Czin said.

The summit is expected to focus on nuclear arms control, with Trump also seeking to discuss the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine. Trump said Monday he intended to raise Ukraine with Xi and Putin, despite administration officials saying last week that the war would not be part of the discussions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern about the prospect of major powers discussing global spheres of influence without Ukraine at the table.

Putin may emerge as the biggest beneficiary of the gathering, Czin said, gaining an opportunity to share the international stage with Trump and Xi despite Russia's isolation from much of the West.

"I think it's a political coup for Putin," Czin said. "Of the three men involved in this meeting, I think he probably is the one who's gaining the most."

Xi also has incentives to participate, Czin said, as the gathering allows Beijing to demonstrate its central role in international affairs while seeking relief from US pressure.

Trump has said he wants to pursue a new nuclear arms agreement that would include China. But Beijing has repeatedly resisted US efforts to engage on nuclear weapons, even as it expands its arsenal.

Czin expects little substantive progress, describing the likely outcome as a superficial exchange rather than the beginning of meaningful arms control negotiations.

The summit comes as Trump seeks to reassert his standing on the world stage following Republican losses in the midterm elections. Czin said the president may see direct engagement with Xi and Putin as an opportunity to demonstrate his influence and build his legacy.

But Trump will also need to show he has not made concessions that undermine US interests, Czin said.

The president must send a clear signal about American priorities and intentions, he said, while reassuring allies that their interests have not been set aside.

For Wang Huiyao, founder and president of the Center for China and Globalization, the gathering represents an opportunity for the three major powers to help shape a new international consensus.

“Last time when China, US and Russian leaders get together, that was 80 some years ago,” he said.

“Now we are at another turning point, we are at a more fragmented world, we are getting to a multipolar world, and the world is lacking strong directions.”

Ukraine war

One area where that could have an immediate impact is the conflict in Ukraine.

Breakthrough is unlikely, yet the three leaders may work out something on which progress can be made at the platforms such as United Nations and G20, said Wang.

"This three leaders' meeting could, you know, kick off some peace consensus that they can really get further strengthened at the UN with the Security Council, other members and even with the European Union and Ukraine to have a peace summit maybe at the UN sometime,” Wang said.

“Then maybe at G20 next month, there could be some even more progress on the ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine," he added.

For Wang Yiwei, Director of the Institute of International Affairs at Renmin University of China, the trialateral summit will only be a complementary effort if the three leaders discussed the Ukraine conflict.

“Ukraine and Russia, these two parts, need to directly negotiate,” he said. “But they're not trusting each other.”

The endorsement from China and US are essential for both sides in the negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, said Wang Yiwei.

The meeting would also underscore China's growing ambitions to play a more active role in international affairs, said Wang Huiyao.

“I think we are coming to a stage that China is the second largest economy, one of the, or probably the second largest military power and even if China is not there, it could also provide guarantor roles, could provide all those active roles there, and all the countries are coming to China and looking for help,” he said.

For Washington, the summit also comes at a politically important moment.

President Trump faces pressure to demonstrate that his foreign and economic policies can deliver results at home, while managing relations with both Beijing and Moscow.

“For President Trump also it is very important because after the ‘Waterloo’ in the midterm election,” said Wang Yiwei.

“So they need to get some beef back and then to show the policy still succeeds," he added.

articles.title: Trump meets regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.summary: Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.
articles.preview: Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative. MANILA: United States President Donald Trump met the leaders of regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, at the start of an Asian trip that also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.
articles.body:
Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.

MANILA: United States President Donald Trump met the leaders of regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, at the start of an Asian trip that also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.

Trump arrived in the Philippine capital at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, and began his three-day regional visit with the first meeting in two years of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific democracies.

"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump said in remarks ahead of the meeting. "We have outstanding relationships and coordinate closely on matters of regional security, economic security and diplomacy."

Trump's three-day Asia trip, which also includes the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen and a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, comes after his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections and spy allegations that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China.

Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.

It was Trump's first meeting of the Quad grouping – which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative – and he said the leaders' discussions would include security and the development of artificial intelligence.

"We want to ensure that the future of this critical technology is dominated by nations that share our values and our common interests and make sure that it turns out to be as good as it can be," Trump said, announcing the Quad would launch a new AI accelerator.

Trump arrived at the end of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and after the Quad meeting will join a US-ASEAN "Special Summit" later on Tuesday.

It comes ahead of the APEC gathering hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

QUAD MEETING THE "BEST POSSIBLE SIGNAL"

At the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed what he called "truly extraordinary" economic achievements of China and ASEAN in the face of global trade restrictions, expressing Beijing's commitment to free trade and the need to "stand united, ward off interference, and work together".

China is ASEAN's biggest trading partner and a key source of investment, but the biggest economies of the 11-member bloc – which has a combined GDP of more than US$3.9 trillion – want to deepen ties with the US despite protracted trade and diplomatic uncertainty under the Trump administration.

Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell credited Washington's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, with the timing and reconvening of the Quad, which he said had lost ambition under Trump.

"Part of what he (Rubio) is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you're going to go into a trilateral meeting," said Campbell, co-founder of The Asia Group, referring to Thursday's US-China-Russia talks.

"The linchpin of everything that we do in Asia is the US-Japan relationship, and a perception that this is not at the top of the president's mind would concern me."

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales on Friday said that under Trump's leadership, the Quad had demonstrated it is "a partnership of action, tackling the region's toughest challenges and driving opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific".

A Japanese foreign ministry official said it was expected that Quad leaders would try to show unity, with maritime security, export restrictions, critical-minerals supply-chain diversification and AI among potential discussion points.

JAPAN TO PLAY MORE PROACTIVE ROLE, PM SAYS

ASEAN’s leaders held meetings on Tuesday involving counterparts of Japan, South Korea, China and India.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to work with ASEAN to boost regional economic and energy resilience to address export restrictions and vulnerabilities from rapid AI development, and strengthen supply chains, including on critical minerals.

“While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play an ever more proactive role,” Takaichi said.

Trump was due to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday on an agreement on reciprocal trade. Thai media have reported the two would hold talks and the statement would be about progress on negotiations.

The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24 per cent of its total shipments this year. The US designated Thailand as a major non-NATO ally in 2003.

Trump will on Wednesday meet Ferdinand Marcos Jr, president of US defence ally the Philippines, before heading to Shenzhen.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.
articles.preview: Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people. Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.

BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.

Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.

Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.

Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.

Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.

His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

articles.title: L’Estonia ha un piano digitale per difendersi dalla Russia
articles.summary: Tallinn sta trasferendo i servizi della pubblica amministrazione sul cloud per mantenere operativo il governo, anche dall’estero, in caso di attacchi informatici o militari
articles.preview: Immaginate il generale francese Charles de Gaulle, in esilio a Londra durante la seconda guerra mondiale, impegnato a dirigere il governo della Francia libera accedendo al cloud. I funzionari estoni si stanno preparando per uno scenario simile con una strategia per rafforzare la capacità di resistere a situazioni catastrofiche (hukukindlus in estone) che permetterà di gestire dall’estero i servizi digitali del governo nel caso di un’occupazione straniera.
articles.body:
Immaginate il generale francese Charles de Gaulle, in esilio a Londra durante la seconda guerra mondiale, impegnato a dirigere il governo della Francia libera accedendo al cloud.

I funzionari estoni si stanno preparando per uno scenario simile con una strategia per rafforzare la capacità di resistere a situazioni catastrofiche (hukukindlus in estone) che permetterà di gestire dall’estero i servizi digitali del governo nel caso di un’occupazione straniera.

Il paese baltico, che ha 1,3 milioni di abitanti e condivide un confine di 294 chilometri con la Russia, teme di diventare uno degli obiettivi principali di Mosca se questa decidesse d’invadere uno stato dell’Unione europea. I servizi di sicurezza hanno più volte avvertito che la Russia sta conducendo una guerra ibrida contro l’Europa, e l’Estonia ha accusato Mosca di attacchi informatici, incendi dolosi e danni ai cavi sottomarini per la trasmissione dei dati.

Ora Tallinn si prepara a trasferire i suoi servizi pubblici sul cloud “nel caso che i data center fossero distrutti o se ci fosse un’occupazione militare che impedisse di operare”, spiega Tõnu Grünberg, uno degli artefici della nuova strategia ed ex vicesegretario generale per le infrastrutture digitali e la cibersicurezza del ministero estone della giustizia e degli affari digitali.

L’Estonia ha già di un backup dei dati nella sua “ambasciata digitale” in Lussemburgo, di fatto una copia di tutti i suoi documenti ufficiali, dai registri anagrafici a quelli catastali fino ai codici delle leggi.

“Ora vogliamo andare davvero online, qualunque cosa accada”, afferma Grünberg. “Tutti i servizi fondamentali dovranno rimanere pienamente operativi”.

Il governo estone sta sviluppando applicazioni sicure su piattaforme cloud come Microsoft Azure e Amazon Web Services, oltre che su una piattaforma statale. Il trasferimento del sistema alla sua ambasciata digitale e ad altre sedi in Europa è in corso, sottolinea Grünberg, che pochi giorni fa ha assunto l’incarico di amministratore delegato della Levira, un’azienda estone d’infrastrutture tecnologiche.

Allan Allmere, consulente per le infrastrutture tecnologiche al ministero della giustizia e degli affari digitali, ha dichiarato a Politico che l’Estonia vuole ridurre al minimo le conseguenze negative anche nello scenario peggiore.

“Idealmente vorremmo realizzare sistemi capaci di resistere a qualunque crisi, ma sappiamo bene che è impossibile prevedere o eliminare del tutto i rischi”, dichiara. “Anche nelle situazioni peggiori, però, dobbiamo avere una base solida per ricostruire lo stato digitale estone”.

Il precedente del 2007

Gli estoni sanno bene che rischi corrono i servizi digitali fin dal 2007, quando per ventidue giorni il paese affrontò un’ondata di attacchi informatici che mise fuori uso buona parte dei servizi privati e della pubblica amministrazione. Le autorità attribuirono gli attacchi alla Russia.

L’episodio, considerato il primo caso di attacco informatico su vasta scala contro uno stato, spinse l’Estonia a riorganizzare completamente le sue infrastrutture digitali, trasformandola in uno dei paesi più digitalizzati del mondo.

“Ha adottato una linea straordinariamente lungimirante in termini di digitalizzazione dei servizi della pubblica amministrazione”, afferma Joseph Jarnecki, ricercatore senior del centro studi Royal united services institute (Rusi) di Londra.

Secondo Allmere, la pianificazione per le situazioni critiche punta a garantire che “non si debba mai ricominciare da zero”.

Gli attacchi recenti ai data center in Russia hanno evidenziato fino a che punto i servizi digitali siano diventati cruciali per i paesi in guerra. Il mese scorso l’Ucraina ha colpito tre data center del provider russo Yandex, dimostrando che gli attacchi di questo tipo hanno ormai un’efficacia paragonabile a quelli contro le centrali da cui dipendono l’elettricità, il riscaldamento e il carburante di militari e civili.

Il piano nazionale estone per la resilienza alle catastrofi è un esempio significativo di come molti paesi stiano cercando di proteggere i propri cittadini e i propri servizi attraverso la delocalizzazione. Fino a poco tempo fa si pensava che fosse più sicuro mantenere il controllo dei servizi digitali all’interno del territorio, archiviando i dati localmente e costruendo tecnologie e data center dentro i confini del paese.

Oggi però gli stati – soprattutto quelli più esposti ai rischi di un conflitto – stanno ripensando questo approccio, in modo da diluire i rischi per le infrastrutture digitali.

Il 12 novembre il Regno Unito e la Norvegia hanno annunciato la possibile creazione di ambasciate digitali nei due paesi per custodire in sicurezza i rispettivi dati.

Anche l’Estonia sta studiando “alleanze con paesi terzi considerati affidabili” per rafforzare la sua sicurezza digitale, “perché non è vero che siamo più forti quando abbiamo tutto all’interno del territorio nazionale”, dice Jarnecki.

L’interruzione dei servizi Microsoft che il 12 novembre ha colpito aziende e governi in tutto il mondo ha evidenziato la necessità per gli stati di diversificare i loro fornitori di servizi cloud e digitali per evitare conseguenze troppo pesanti in caso di attacchi informatici o problemi tecnici.

Secondo Allmere, il governo estone è pronto ad affrontare nuove sfide. “La prima era assicurarsi che i dati dello stato non andassero persi”, dice riferendosi all’ambasciata digitale in Lussemburgo che fa da backup. “La prossima sarà garantire che lo stato continui a funzionare, grazie a quegli stessi dati, nell’eventualità di una crisi”.

Ma non basta. “Dobbiamo essere sicuri che i dati rimangano leggibili e utilizzabili anche tra decenni”, conclude Allmere. ◆

articles.title: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
articles.summary: Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.
articles.preview: November 16, 2026 Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country. "I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW. Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.
articles.body:
November 16, 2026

Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.

"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.

Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.

"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.

"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."

She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.

Turkey as a stopover

"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."

Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.

Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

A US naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.

The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.

The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.

She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."

Young Iranians lose faith in the future

The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.

A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.

The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.

Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.

Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.

"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Algeria threatens to target drug traffickers at 'source' amid Morocco tensions
articles.summary: Algeria is declaring war on drugs. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune is threatening tougher action, warning that the fight must target the source of the problem.
articles.preview: news Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Sunday threatened to take action against drugs at "the source" amid longstanding accusations by Algiers that neighbouring Morocco was behind drug trafficking into the country. Tebboune did not name Morocco in an address at the Algerian Supreme Court, but Algiers has often blamed Morocco as being the source of drugs trafficked through their shared border. "It's a war declared against Algeria, and when there's war the army is of course at the front line," Tebboune said.
articles.body:
news

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Sunday threatened to take action against drugs at "the source" amid longstanding accusations by Algiers that neighbouring Morocco was behind drug trafficking into the country.

Tebboune did not name Morocco in an address at the Algerian Supreme Court, but Algiers has often blamed Morocco as being the source of drugs trafficked through their shared border. "It's a war declared against Algeria, and when there's war the army is of course at the front line," Tebboune said. "If necessary, we can go further, even to the source of the drugs' production, in legitimate self-defence."

On Thursday, authorities said they destroyed nearly 10 tonnes of recently seized cannabis resin as well as 33 million psychotropic pills, although it remained unclear where the drugs had come from. Relations between Algeria and Morocco have been tense since Algiers severed diplomatic ties in 2021.

Last month, Tebboune also said drug trafficking into Algeria was part of a "hybrid war" waged by "saboteurs", although he again did not name any actors. The Algerian defence ministry regularly announces confiscating large amounts of drugs, with statements often saying they came from Morocco.

articles.title: Come è nata la falsa notizia del blackout globale del 17 novembre
articles.summary: È un allarme privo di prove che fa leva sulla preoccupazione dei recenti attacchi informatici
articles.preview: Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.
articles.body:
Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.

Un allarme che fa leva sulla preoccupazione degli attacchi informatici delle scorse settimane in diversi Paesi europei, dei (falsi) allarmi bomba negli aeroporti e nelle scuole, e del problema informatico che ha bloccato per diversi tempo i servizi di Microsoft.

Ma di questo blackout del 17 novembre, non esistono prove. Questa storia, del tutto infondata, è nata travisando alcuni eventi recenti reali. Il primo riguarda le nuove linee guida della Commissione europea, presentate lo scorso 3 novembre al Forum europeo sulla protezione civile, per aiutare le persone a prepararsi alle emergenze ed essere autosufficienti per 72 ore, durante i primi giorni di un’eventuale crisi. Le linee guida arrivano a seguito dell’approvazione a marzo 2025 della Strategia dell’Unione europea in materia di preparazione. La Commissione ha proposto anche l’istituzione di una Giornata europea della preparazione alle emergenze, ma a partire dal prossimo anno, il 2027, e il 23 ottobre (non il 17 novembre). Da tempo documenti delle istituzioni europee o frasi dei suoi rappresentanti vengono manipolati in rete per diffondere tesi complottistiche di vario genere.

La data del 17 novembre ipotizzata dai contenuti social allarmistici arriva invece dagli Stati Uniti. Nel Paese, infatti, martedì le emittenti radiofoniche e televisive interromperanno la normale programmazione per trasmettere un messaggio di prova. Si tratta di un test triennale per verificare la funzionalità del sistema di allarme in caso di una reale emergenza nazionale. A svolgerlo sarà l’Ente federale per la gestione delle emergenze (FEMA), e ne aveva dato annuncio lo scorso settembre la Commissione federale per le comunicazioni (FCC).

Secondo poi diversi post questo fantomatico blackout globale del 17 novembre sarebbe stato profetizzato dai Simpson. Un episodio della serie televisiva statunitense – a cui sono stati attribuiti poteri divinatori per alcune coincidenze con la realtà – avrebbe infatti rivelato questa data di un prossimo blackout. Si tratta del settimo episodio della 35ª stagione, andato in onda originariamente il 19 novembre 2023 e intitolato “It’s a Blunderful Life”, in cui una Lisa Simpson adulta ripensa a un’interruzione di corrente che lasciò Springfield al buio per sei giorni, avvenuta proprio il 17 novembre.

Tuttavia, nell’episodio non viene specificato l’anno del blackout, e l’interruzione di corrente – della durata di sei giorni – termina il Giorno del Ringraziamento. Nel 2026 però questa festività cade il 26 novembre, ovvero 9 giorni più tardi la data del blackout ipotizzato. Inoltre, nell’episodio il blackout colpisce solo la cittadina di Springfield e non tutto il pianeta. Anche questo caso rientra quindi nel filone disinformativo che attribuisce ai Simpson poteri divinatori a causa di alcune coincidenze occorse nelle oltre 700 puntate andate in onda.

articles.title: Scattered by war, the band that gave voice to Sudan's revolution plays again
articles.summary: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.preview: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.body:
Sudan

The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered them across multiple continents.

After living through revolution, war and years of displacement, Mustafa and his fellow musicians in "Aswat al-Madina" (Arabic for Voices of the City) have reunited in the Egyptian capital, returning to both recording and live performance.

"I still can't quite process the fact that we're back together," said Mustafa, the band's guitarist and co-founder, who goes by Timon.

"It still feels unreal," he told AFP between recording takes, as back home war rages between the two forces Sudan's youth once rallied against: the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

In the studio, old stories and songs transport the musicians back to Khartoum, where they became the soundtrack to Sudan's 2018 uprising against longtime ruler Omar al-Bashir.

Two days before war erupted between the army and the RSF, former allies who worked together to derail Sudan's transition to democracy, the band was debating setlists for their next performance.

Instead, they found themselves swept up in the conflict, which has since devastated Sudan, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing millions more.

'Never left me'

Founded in Khartoum in 2014, Aswat al-Madina was part of a wave of underground bands pushing Sudanese music beyond conventional boundaries.

Blending folk traditions with jazz, reggae and contemporary rhythms, they sang about corruption, social injustice and life under authoritarian rule.

"Before the revolution, we used a technique where everyone understood what we meant, but nobody could prove it," said lead singer Ibrahim Ahmed Taha, who was arrested several times over their music.

When Sudan's youth took to the streets in December 2018, demanding an end to Bashir's rule, the band's songs blasted from phones, passing cars and makeshift barricades.

Timon still remembers one demonstrator carrying a giant speaker blaring their music through the marches.

"The music pushed people forward. It told them not to retreat in the face of repression.

"That image has never left me."

The band was a regular fixture at pro-democracy protests, including at the sit-in outside military headquarters in Khartoum, where protesters gathered each evening to listen to speeches, poetry and music.

"Find me in the square at half-past revolution; tonight, the devil falls," one track goes.

That sit-in became the site of a massacre in June 2019, when security forces led by the military and the RSF killed at least 120 protesters.

Four years later, when those same forces turned their guns on each other, the band -- like many Sudanese - lost everything.

From their five-storey creative hub, "everything was gone," Timon said.

"Not just the musical equipment. Even the chairs and tables had been looted."

"You'd step into the street and see bodies lying there and buildings reduced to rubble. That's when you realise everything has fallen apart," Timon said.

As fighting spread, the musicians fled Sudan, carrying little more than backpacks and laptops.

'In Khartoum again'

Timon escaped to the United Arab Emirates while others settled in Egypt and elsewhere in Africa. Regular rehearsals gave way to anxious discussions of visas and relatives still trapped in Sudan.

It was only this August that the band could reunite in Cairo, for its first performance since the war began.

As familiar songs filled the venue, audience members sang along to every word, shouting requests.

"For a moment," Taha said, "I felt like I was in Khartoum again."

For keyboard player Roba Bashir, the band's only woman member, the reunion was "the happiest day since the war began".

Musab Mahgoub, who has attended two of the band's Cairo concerts since August, said the performances "brought back so many old memories of Sudan".

The band now hopes to tour internationally and is recording a new version of their song "Nos Kobayet Shai Bi'Aisha" ("Half a Cup of Tea with Bread") with an Egyptian-Nubian collaborator, its themes of home and family taking on special meaning in exile.

APEC countries are focused on the safe deployment and responsible application of artificial intelligence, Chen Xu, the chair of the APEC Senior Officials' Meeting this year, said on Tuesday (Nov 17).

SHENZHEN: Countries making up the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) are focused on the safe deployment and responsible application of artificial intelligence, Chen Xu, the chair of the APEC Senior Officials' Meeting this year, said on Tuesday (Nov 17).

APEC members have had an in-depth discussion and reached an important consensus around AI-related issues, said Chen, who was China's ambassador to the United Nations until last year.

His comments come as China and the United States, the world's two largest economies, are in a race over leadership in AI while their technology ties grow more strained.

"In the realms of digital technology and AI, the parties engaged in in-depth discussions on a wide range of issues including... the safe deployment and responsible application of AI," Chen told a press conference.

He added the member states had discussed for the first time the role of data in driving AI growth.

The US on Monday tightened restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing advanced US AI chips through overseas data centers, a loophole Washington says could allow firms to circumvent existing export controls.
